question: Through sustainable fisheries partnership agreements (SFPAs), the EU facilitates access for EU fleets to tuna stocks in the waters of non-EU countries. Concurrently, the recovering eastern stock of Atlantic bluefin tuna is returning to the North Sea.

Small-scale EU coastal fishers cannot benefit from this recovery, as national quota allocations rely on historical catch records rather than the current distribution of species. The absence of by-catch arrangements forces them to discard incidental catches, thus undermining the landing obligation. Meanwhile, the UK, having acquired a quota share, has opened a tuna fishery to small-scale vessels.

Although quota allocation remains a national competence, Article 17 of the Common Fisheries Policy Regulation requires the Member States to apply socio-economic and environmental criteria when allocating fishing opportunities. 1.

How does the Commission assess the policy imbalance whereby the EU extensively supports international tuna fishing, yet provides no active framework to assist smallscale North Sea fishers in benefiting from locally returning stocks of Atlantic bluefin tuna?

In the light of its vade mecum on Article 171 and the upcoming simplification package, how will the Commission monitor and support Member States in applying this guidance to grant small-scale fishers access to emerging stocks via by-catch or trial quotas?

How does the Commission intend to address, at the upcoming annual meeting of the International Commission for the Conservation of Atlantic Tunas (ICCAT), the geographical scope of artisanal quota provisions in relation to northern EU waters?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (28.9.2026) The EU is committed to the sustainable exploitation of all marine living resources, both domestically and internationally. Therefore, there is no imbalance between the two policy aspects. The legal framework1 gives Member States the responsibility to decide the allocation systems to distribute opportunities to the vessels flying their flag.

The Commission has no competence to oblige Member States to allocate fishing opportunities to small-scale fishers. The mentioned vade mecum2 aimed to bring to the forefront of the national policy dialogues the allocation of fishing opportunities to support small-scale fishers.

The Commission has observed that several Member States have taken concrete steps towards reforming their national allocation mechanisms to better integrate emerging social and environmental considerations, including the allocation of bluefin tuna (BFT) quota to their small-scale fishers. Clearly, further discussions with Member States are needed to encourage them to follow the example.

No specific framework exists in the context of the International Commission for the Conservation of Atlantic Tunas (ICCAT) for allocating fishing opportunities to artisanal fisheries. ICCAT sets the overall catch limit for eastern bluefin tuna in accordance with the management procedure, and it decides on the allocation of these fishing opportunities among ICCAT Contracting Parties.

Last year, a new catch limit for BFT was set for 2026, 2027 and 2028, which saw a 17% increase in the EU’s fishing opportunities. The Council decides on any changes of fishing opportunities among Member States.
1 Articles 16 and 17 of the Common Fisheries Policy Regulation. 2 2025 Communication form the Commission for enhanced transparency and good governance in the allocation

of fishing opportunities by Member States: A vade mecum on the application of Articles 16 and 17 of Regulation (EU) No 1380/2013 on the Common Fisheries Policy [Brussels, 14.11.2025 C(2025) 7655] https://eurlex.europa.eu/eli/C/2025/6227/oj.
